strengths: The practical goal is valuable: combining pretrained visual generators, VLM rewards, and simulator-derived controls without retraining offers flexible interfaces for image editing and video generation.

The experiments demonstrate promising control improvements. Foreground LPIPS improves from 0.178 to 0.065 for image insertion, and from 0.164 for Depth2V to 0.136 on the full-scene video benchmark, alongside improved GPT-4o quality scores.
The paper includes useful qualitative examples, an ablation of conditional updates, and implementation details covering model checkpoints, resolutions, sampling schedules, and approximate runtimes.
weaknesses: The claimed sampling interpretation is not established. Algorithm 1 omits AIS importance corrections and does not derive valid incremental SMC weights for its actual transition kernels. Repeatedly resampling using the current reward after finite generative-only MCMC updates does not generally target Equation (6). Appendix E.2 further replaces probabilistic weighting with median-threshold duplication and final maximum-score selection. These are useful search heuristics, but they do not substantiate sampling from the stated product distribution.

There are additional mathematical inconsistencies in the implementation. Appendix D.1's velocity-to-score conversion does not match the standard identity for the stated Gaussian probability path. Spatially masking and normalizing expert scores also need not produce the gradient of any joint log density, much less the unweighted product in Equation (1). Appendix D.2 does not adequately justify converting its flow-consistency energy into the velocity update in Equation (7). These issues directly affect the central probabilistic claim.

Evaluation is too limited for the breadth of the claims: 30 image scenes constructed from only 10 backgrounds and three objects, 12 object-centric video scenes, and nine full-scene video scenes. Most importantly, the combined generative/discriminative framework is demonstrated through only two text-to-image examples, without aggregate benchmark results. The quantitative image and video experiments use one particle and therefore do not validate the proposed SMC component.

The image-editing comparison is confounded by unequal conditioning: RF-Solver receives an image and coarse text, while the proposed method receives precise geometry and masks through specialized experts. Comparisons against individual conditioned experts, sequential combinations, and straightforward masked blending using the same inputs are needed. Related compositional diffusion and SMC methods are discussed but not experimentally compared.

Physical accuracy and sample efficiency are not convincingly measured. LPIPS to renderings, smoothness, and GPT-4o judgments do not directly establish trajectory or collision accuracy. Object-centric controllability ties Image2V under GPT-4o and is slightly worse than Depth2V under LPIPS. There are no quantitative success-versus-compute curves or systematic comparisons with rejection sampling or best-of-N generation.

The methodological novelty remains insufficiently distinguished from existing PoE diffusion composition, annealed MCMC, regional generation, and SMC reward steering. The heterogeneous integration is potentially useful, but stronger matched comparisons and component ablations are needed to show that the proposed framework contributes more than an application-specific combination of established techniques.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied implementation details: key parameters such as Langevin step sizes and conditional-update strengths are unspecified, evaluation assets and seeds are not adequately documented, and baseline runtimes are absent. The supplied manuscript also refers to supplementary videos that cannot be assessed from the PDF.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining pretrained visual generators, VLM feedback, and simulation-derived controls without retraining. The image editing and video applications demonstrate practical flexibility.

There are encouraging empirical results. Foreground LPIPS improves from 0.178 to 0.065 for image insertion, and from 0.164 for Depth2V to 0.136 on the full-scene video benchmark. The conditional-update ablation also supports improved visual harmonization.
The manuscript provides backbone identities, inference configurations, approximate runtimes, and qualitative ablations, and acknowledges computational overhead and expert incompatibility.
weaknesses: The central sampling interpretation is not established. Algorithm 1 uses short generative-only MCMC updates followed by resampling with absolute discriminator rewards, without deriving the incremental importance weights or transition corrections needed to target Eq. (6). Appendix E.2 actually uses median-threshold pruning and duplication, followed by maximum-reward selection. These procedures can provide useful heuristic search, but do not generally sample the claimed product distribution. With only one MCMC step per iteration, an assumption of complete equilibration cannot justify the discrepancy.

The practical vector fields are not shown to correspond to the stated probability distributions. Spatially masking and normalizing expert scores generally does not preserve the score of the unweighted PoE, and coordinate-wise masking can produce a nonconservative field. Appendix D.1 also appears to give an incorrect velocity-to-score conversion: for a Gaussian interpolation, the score is obtained by subtracting the linear-in-x drift from the velocity and dividing by the scheduler coefficient, rather than the expression printed there. Appendix D.2 does not adequately justify converting its compatibility energy into the conditional velocity update in Eq. (7). These issues require correction and validation.

Evaluation is too limited for the breadth of the claims: image insertion uses 30 combinations of 10 images and three objects; video evaluation uses 12 object-centric scenes and nine full-scene scenes. The experiment combining generative and discriminative experts—the most distinctive part of the framework—has only two qualitative prompt examples, with no aggregate benchmark results or independent quantitative assessment.

Baseline coverage and input matching are insufficient. RF-Solver receives image and text, while the proposed image editor additionally receives precise geometry through depth conditioning; the paper explicitly acknowledges this disparity. Thus, the comparison does not isolate the value of the proposed sampler. Comparisons against existing compositional generation and SMC steering methods, and simpler combinations of the same experts with identical controls, are missing. The compute-matched best-of-N comparison is restricted to qualitative examples.

Claims of improved physical accuracy and controllability exceed the measurements. LPIPS against rendered frames and GPT-4o judgments do not directly establish trajectory accuracy, collision consistency, or physical validity. In the object-centric setting, the proposed method slightly trails Depth2V on LPIPS and ties Image2V on GPT-4o controllability. Standard deviations are reported, but repeated-seed results and paired uncertainty estimates are absent.

The methodological novelty over existing PoE composition, annealed MCMC, and SMC reward steering is insufficiently isolated. Moreover, sample-efficiency claims lack quantitative quality-versus-compute curves or systematic ablations of MCMC steps, particle counts, and resampling. Although approximate runtimes are disclosed, key numerical choices such as the Langevin step size and conditional-update weight are not clearly specified, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: combining pretrained visual generators, semantic evaluators, and simulation-derived controls without retraining. The image-editing and video-generation applications demonstrate useful flexibility.

The reported results show promising improvements. In Table 1, foreground LPIPS improves from 0.178 to 0.065 over RF-Solver; on PhysGen3D scenes, Table 2 reports better LPIPS and GPT-4o video-quality scores than the neural baselines.

The conditional-update ablation provides some evidence of improved visual harmonization and text alignment. The appendix also specifies model checkpoints, resolutions, sampling schedules, hardware, and approximate runtimes.
weaknesses: The claimed sampling interpretation is not established. Algorithm 1 lacks AIS importance-weight corrections and does not derive SMC incremental weights accounting for its transitions and previously applied rewards. One unadjusted Langevin step does not produce an independent draw from each intermediate generative distribution. Moreover, Appendix E.2 uses median-threshold selection and particle duplication, followed by maximum-reward selection. These operations are heuristic search procedures, not justified sampling from the stated product distribution.

There are additional inconsistencies between the probabilistic formulation and implementation. Appendix D.1's velocity-to-score equation appears algebraically incorrect: for the stated Gaussian interpolation, v = (α̇/α)x + ((α̇/α)σ² − σ̇σ)s, which must be inverted to obtain s. Spatially masked, normalized score blending also need not be the gradient of the log density in Eq. (1). Appendix D.2 does not adequately justify converting its conditional score correction directly into the velocity update in Eq. (7). These issues affect the central technical account.

The image-editing comparison is substantially confounded by unequal conditioning. The proposed method receives explicit geometry through a depth expert and uses an inpainting expert, whereas RF-Solver receives an image and coarse text. Better pose adherence therefore does not isolate the benefit of the proposed sampler. Comparisons against methods receiving the same controls, and against simple expert blending without MCMC, are needed.

Evaluation is too limited for the breadth of the claims: 30 image-editing scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, and nine full-scene simulations. The text-to-image experiment—the main demonstration combining generative and discriminative experts—contains only two qualitative examples, without aggregate benchmark results. The compute-matched best-of-N comparison consequently provides little evidence of general sample-efficiency gains.

Evidence for improved physical accuracy is indirect. LPIPS, generic video-quality metrics, and GPT-4o judgments do not directly measure trajectory error, collision consistency, or physical dynamics. Results are also mixed: on object-centric videos, controllability ties Image2V under GPT-4o and foreground LPIPS is slightly worse than Depth2V. Reported standard deviations do not establish the reliability of the differences.

Novelty beyond existing compositional diffusion, MCMC composition, regional generation, and SMC reward steering is insufficiently isolated. Missing quantitative ablations of MCMC, resampling, expert composition, and particle count make it difficult to identify the essential contribution. Reproduction is further limited by unspecified Langevin step sizes and conditional-update weights.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining pretrained visual models, VLM rewards, and simulation-derived controls without retraining. Demonstrations span object insertion, physics-guided video generation, and layout-controlled image generation.

Several results show practical benefits. Conditional updates improve object-insertion controllability, and composing video experts improves GPT-4o quality scores over individual experts. The qualitative examples illustrate improved control while retaining plausible scene appearance.

The paper includes same-backbone application baselines, conditional-sampling and resampling ablations, particle-count scaling, and hardware/runtime disclosures. Table 4 provides evidence that intermediate resampling improves reward scores over the reported no-SMC variant at comparable cost.
weaknesses: The central sampling justification is not established. Algorithm 1 uses finite MCMC transitions without AIS importance corrections, repeatedly resamples using the current reward rather than a derived sequential importance ratio, and finally selects the highest-reward particle. An invariant kernel does not imply that a finite transition produces an equilibrium sample, especially with only one MCMC step in the experiments. Reweighting by the reward would be justified after exact sampling from the generative product, but that condition is not demonstrated. The final maximum-reward selection also differs from sampling the stated product distribution. These distinctions undermine the claimed principled AIS/SMC interpretation.

The implemented updates further depart from the stated probabilistic model. Appendix C.1 uses unadjusted finite-step Langevin dynamics, which generally does not exactly preserve the target density. It also replaces the sum of expert scores with normalized, spatially weighted scores; these need not correspond to the product in Eq. (3), or even to a conservative score field. Appendix C.3 derives a score correction but applies it directly as a velocity correction in Eq. (6), without establishing the required conversion. The method may be an effective heuristic, but its claimed target distribution is unclear.

The strongest layout-alignment results use VQAScore both as the steering/selection reward and as the principal evaluation metric, including regional scores. This demonstrates optimization of the chosen evaluator, but does not independently establish better semantic fidelity. Human judgments or a held-out evaluator are needed. Independent mIoU gains are smaller, and Table 4 shows that resampling actually reduces mIoU at L = 4 and L = 8.

Evaluation breadth exceeds its statistical depth: graphics insertion uses 30 scenes, object-centric video uses 12, full-scene video uses nine, and layout generation uses only 50 of 800 benchmark scenes. Repeated-seed uncertainty and paired significance analyses are absent. Improvements are also mixed: Depth2V achieves better foreground IoU than the proposed method, while other insertion methods outperform it on background preservation or foreground similarity.

Comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution over existing composition methods. The graphics-insertion baseline receives textual placement instructions while the proposed method receives precise geometric controls. Closely related SMC/Feynman–Kac composition methods are discussed but not experimentally compared. Quantitative compute-matched comparisons with stronger selection/composition baselines are needed to substantiate novelty and efficiency, especially when layout generation takes approximately 25 minutes at 32 particles.

The claimed autoregressive generality and reproducibility are insufficiently supported. Appendix C.2 is empty, and the autoregressive experiment uses sampling followed by eight simulation-loss gradient updates rather than a demonstrated Gibbs kernel or MAP optimization of the full product. Evidence is qualitative only. Important settings, including Langevin step sizes and conditional-update strengths, are not specified, and the project-page link is blank.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining pretrained generators, semantic rewards, and simulation-derived controls without retraining. Demonstrations span image insertion, layout-controlled generation, and video generation.

There are meaningful empirical gains. On layout generation, the 32-particle configuration improves mIoU from 0.673 to 0.728 and VQAScore from 0.800 to 0.904 relative to 3DIS-FLUX. Image-editing examples also demonstrate improved object placement and harmonization.

The conditional-guidance and resampling ablations provide useful evidence about individual components. Table 4 includes equal-particle-count comparisons without resampling, and the appendix reports hardware and approximate runtimes.
weaknesses: The claimed sampling justification does not establish that Algorithm 1 targets the stated product distribution. Invariance of an intermediate MCMC kernel does not make a finite transition produce samples from its stationary distribution; experiments typically use only one step. Repeated weighting by the full discriminator reward lacks the incremental importance-weight correction or derivation needed for the stated target. Final maximum-reward selection further changes the output distribution. The median-threshold duplication procedure in Appendix D.5 is also different from the probabilistic resampling described in the main algorithm.

The implemented generative updates depart from the mathematical formulation. Appendix C.1 uses spatially weighted score averages whose weights sum to one, rather than the score sum required by Equation (3). Coordinate-dependent masking need not yield a conservative score field at all. Its unadjusted finite-step Langevin kernel also does not exactly preserve the claimed target. These discrepancies undermine the paper's central distinction from prior methods that explicitly correct sampling weights.

The conditional and autoregressive constructions are insufficiently justified. Appendix C.3 introduces a flow-consistency energy but does not adequately derive its conversion into the velocity update in Equation (6). Section C.2, which should explain autoregressive sampling, is empty. The actual autoregressive implementation samples from FramePack and applies eight simulation-loss gradient updates; this does not establish Gibbs sampling or MAP inference for the full product containing the generative prior.

The strongest semantic evaluation reuses the optimization reward: VQAScore supplies both particle-selection guidance and the reported global/regional alignment metrics. These gains demonstrate improved reward optimization but require independent evaluation to establish broader semantic improvement. No human evaluation or independent semantic judge is reported for this task.

Evaluation coverage and uncertainty are limited: 30 graphics scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, nine full-scene simulations, and only 50 of 800 MIG-Bench scenes. Results lack repeated-seed analysis or significance estimates. Gains are also mixed: Depth2V achieves higher foreground IoU than the proposed method, while FLUX-Fill preserves image backgrounds better and SDEdit achieves better foreground LPIPS.

Several comparisons do not isolate the contribution. RF-Solver receives textual placement instructions while the proposed method receives explicit geometric controls. There are no direct experimental comparisons against the closely related heterogeneous composition and SMC methods discussed in Section 2. The quantitative layout comparison also lacks a compute-matched best-of-N 3DIS-FLUX baseline; the no-resampling ablation only partially addresses this concern.

Efficiency and reproducibility claims need stronger support. Layout generation takes approximately 12–25 minutes at 16–32 particles, without comparable baseline timings or quality-versus-compute curves. Important parameters, including Langevin step size and conditional-guidance strength, are not specified. Overall, the practical demonstrations are promising, but the unresolved sampling formulation and evaluation limitations fall below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining pretrained visual generators, discriminative rewards, and simulator-derived controls without retraining. Applications span image insertion, motion-controlled video generation, and layout-conditioned synthesis.

Results demonstrate promising practical benefits. On character insertion, the method improves aesthetic score, ImageReward, and GPT-4o controllability over the reported baselines. Layout generation improves mIoU from 0.673 for 3DIS-FLUX to 0.728 with 32 particles.

The conditional-update ablation and SMC ablation provide useful evidence about individual components. The appendix reports hardware, runtimes, and several implementation settings, and the qualitative examples illustrate the intended controls clearly.
weaknesses: The central sampling justification is incomplete. Algorithm 1 repeatedly weights particles by the current reward after finite generative-only MCMC updates, without deriving the incremental importance weights needed for its actual proposals. Invariance of a kernel does not imply that one step produces a sample from its stationary distribution. Moreover, Appendix C.1 uses unadjusted finite-step Langevin updates, which do not generally preserve the claimed target exactly. Final maximum-reward selection and the median-based pruning in Appendix D.5 further depart from sampling Eq. (1). These choices may be useful heuristics, but the stated AIS/SMC interpretation is not established.

The implemented composition differs materially from the stated product distribution. Appendix C.1 normalizes spatial expert weights to sum to one, whereas Eq. (3) requires the sum of expert scores. Even constant scalar averaging changes the target to a tempered product; coordinate-dependent masking need not yield a valid joint score. Appendix C.3 also does not adequately justify converting its conditional-density score correction directly into the velocity update in Eq. (6).

Evaluation of discriminative steering is substantially coupled to the optimization objective: VQAScore supplies both the selection reward and the principal semantic evaluation metrics. Independent semantic evaluation or blinded human judgments are needed. Although Table 4 includes a useful No-SMC comparison, compute-matched best-of-N generation is illustrated only qualitatively, and comparisons with the closely related composition and SMC methods discussed in Section 2 are missing.

The evaluation sets are small: 30 graphics-insertion scenes, 80 character combinations from demo assets, 12 object-centric videos, nine full-scene videos, and 50 of 800 MIG-Bench scenes. Some controls are also unequal: RF-Solver receives textual placement instructions while the proposed method receives explicit geometry. Results show tradeoffs rather than uniform superiority; for example, Depth2V achieves higher foreground IoU than the proposed method, 0.787 versus 0.739.

The claimed generality and efficiency exceed the evidence. Most image-editing and video experiments use one particle, so they do not validate the combined discriminative-resampling framework. The autoregressive demonstration is qualitative and replaces sampling with simulator-loss optimization; its promised technical subsection C.2 is empty. Layout generation reaches approximately 25 minutes per image at 32 particles, without a corresponding baseline quality-versus-runtime comparison.

The practical integration is promising, but PoE composition, annealed MCMC, and SMC reward steering are established ingredients. Without a sound derivation of the proposed combination and stronger controlled comparisons, the methodological advance and empirical evidence are insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
